verdict.rationale: React's own docs say it can render on the server, stream HTML while data is still being fetched, and progressively fill in content before any JavaScript loads. hydrateRoot then attaches React to that server-rendered HTML to make it interactive. The evidence covers server rendering, streaming and hydration, but not the 'faster interactivity' outcome or the streaming API itself, and React steers full apps toward frameworks like Next.js. missing for 10: API-level docs for the streaming server renderer (e.g. a react-dom/server streaming method), evidence that streaming or selective hydration speeds up time-to-interactive, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, I can render my application on the server with streaming support to reach interactivity faster

citations.quote: On the server, React lets you start streaming HTML while you’re still fetching data, progressively filling in the remaining content before any JavaScript code loads.
React can also render on the server using Node
Call `hydrateRoot` to “attach” React to existing HTML that was already rendered by React in a server environment.
hydrateRoot lets you display React components inside a browser DOM node whose HTML content was previously generated by react-dom/server.
